en: The Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra: A Compendium.

The words of this sūtra are few, yet the Way it reveals is vast; its expressions are subtle, yet their purport is profound. It is truly the bright lamp for sentient beings throughout the long night and the very life-force of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
If one studies it and grasps its essential meaning, one will be able to govern the single body and command the myriad phenomena.
Transformation. Whether for one's own benefit or the benefit of others, whether entering the mundane or the supramundane, there is nothing to which it is not well-suited.
To investigate its essential point, it lies in the single phrase: "perceiving that the five aggregates are all empty. This constitutes the core of the entire sutra.

Generally speaking, the reason the Way is not clearly understood and the mind is difficult to discipline is rooted entirely in the mark of self (*ātman*). The Tathāgata, knowing that the poison of the mark of self is exceedingly great, therefore [proceeded] with this very...

From nature, one opens up into form and mind; from form and mind, one opens up into the five aggregates (*skandhas*); from the five aggregates, one opens up into the twelve bases (*āyatanas*) and eighteen elements (*dhātus*).

Furthermore, these are detailed as the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). When one investigates their ultimate destination, they do not transcend the two dharmas of form and mind.
As for the essence of the mental dharma, it takes wisdom and attainment together as its ultimate, which is non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Alas, ordinary beings lack this.
People often say that Buddhism is empty and unreal; they do not realize that the Buddha-dharma is, in fact, true and not false.

This is because what is being taught is precisely intended to eliminate the unreality of delusion and establish the reality of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*). The "emptiness" spoken of refers merely to the emptiness of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*);
what remains is the fundamental nature itself. Failing to distinguish between nature and characteristics, people cling to various illusory appearances and thus remain mired in worldly folly.

For humanity, calamity has persisted from antiquity to the present. Indulging their passions and following their delusions, they drift and sink in the ocean of suffering, appearing and disappearing without constancy, changing heads and faces, and growing feathers and fur haphazardly—how could there ever be an end to this? Therefore, our Buddha sought to lead people away from the emptiness of folly and delusion.

Establishing the reality of the fundamental nature, the Dharma is taught and pointed out; the true aspect is discussed in secret. If the light of the mind does not radiate, the ocean of nature will not be clarified.
The mind is not a separate function, and the sutras are not a separate teaching. Taking contemplative observation as the primary principle, one returns to wisdom where both are forgotten;
this is the definitive meaning of ultimate truth. Now, if one’s ground of insight is clear yet one does not cultivate contemplative practice, how is this different from [having no insight at all]?
If the fields are not plowed and contemplative practice is not cultivated, the mind will inevitably encounter obstructions and fail to attain mastery.

Ignorance will blaze fiercely and emotional consciousness will become rigidly bound, such that the primordial light of wisdom will be utterly buried and lost. (Nianqu) Having early studied the vehicles of the teachings, I have fortunately not yet fallen into the pits and ditches;
yet, with black hair suddenly turning white, the realm of sorrow has snatched away my joy. Reflecting quietly upon my life thus far, it is as if...
As if in a dream, while compiling this scripture, my tears involuntarily welled up.

Although the days remaining until my end are few, I still wish to urge myself on with diligent self-exhortation, so that at the final stage of my path, I may uproot the deep-seated emotional roots of long kalpas. This is the compilation of this work.

Having extensively searched and widely gathered [these materials] over many years, their principles are refined and their explanations complete. May those who study them with diligent inquiry and cultivate them through repeated practice find some small benefit.
This work has been carved alongside the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and five thousand and forty-eight volumes have been solicited for printing.
May this be widely circulated so as not to辜负 (fail) the compassionate intention of our Buddha to universally deliver all beings.
The sages of the Three Teachings all spoke of the mind through their teachings; immeasurable sentient beings can all achieve fulfillment by means of these teachings.

May readers clarify the mind through the teachings, transform the various consciousnesses to realize true wisdom, and transcend empty and illusory appearances to awaken to the True Principle. This very mind is...
The Buddha is truly eternal and unimpeded; his wondrous awakening is perfectly luminous. How could there be any suffering or calamity that he does not deliver?
Recorded on the first day of the seventh month in the year of Jiayin, the fifty-ninth year of the Qianlong era, by Sun Nianqu, a humble descendant of Shu Fu.
Yuanqi Xianshou takes this sutra to be spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha. Xuanzhu says: "This was spoken by the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Shihu’s original version states: "The World-Honored One was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, having entered the profound light..."
[The Buddha] spoke. Having finished expounding the samādhi of the True Dharma, Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"If there are those who wish to practice and study this profound gateway of the Prajñāpāramitā, how should they practice and study it?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara spoke this sūtra; this sūtra is a great section of the Prajñāpāramitā spoken by the World-Honored One.
As for its essential core, one should know that the discourse of the Bodhisattva is, in fact, the speech of the World-Honored One. Avalokiteśvara is none other than Guanshiyin;

he attained Buddhahood in the past under the name Zhengfaming (Vairocana), yet he has since receded to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) to assist the Buddha in his transformative activities.
Having long practiced the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he was about to expound the essence of the mind; thus, the sutra first describes his own [realization].
It is practiced because its expression is not false.
When the Heart Sūtra reached the Eastern Land, it underwent five translations in total.

The first was translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin dynasty, titled the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāmahāvidyāmantra-sūtra* (the number of characters and phrases differs slightly from Xuanzang’s version). The second was by Xuanzang of the Tang...

1. Translated by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty, titled *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*; this is the version currently in circulation (consisting of fifty-four phrases and two hundred and sixty-eight characters;
among the five translations, only this one has survived). 2. Translated by Yijing of the Tang dynasty, titled the same as that of Master Xuanzang. 3.
Translated by Dharmachandra of the Song dynasty, titled *Samantaprajñājñānagarbha-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. 4. Translated by Dānapāla of the Song dynasty.
It is titled *The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Noble Mother Prajñāpāramitā*. In the Tibetan canon, only the two translations by Kumārajīva and Xuanzang are recorded;

the other versions are not included [among the five, only Xuanzang’s translation has been widely circulated]. First, it accords with antiquity, as its literary style and meaning are particularly excellent; since ancient times, all have venerated this version. Second, it is practical for use:

when Master Xuanzang traveled to and from the Western Regions, he relied solely upon this text to dispel demonic obstacles. The *Biographies of Divine Monks* states that when Master Xuanzang was traveling westward and reached the kingdom of Kaśmīra, the road was so perilous that he could not pass. There he encountered an elderly monk who orally transmitted this [text] to him.

The scriptures caused Xuanzang to recite them, whereby the mountains and rivers became level, the roads were opened, tigers and leopards hid their forms, and malevolent spirits and demons vanished from sight; thus he was able to reach the Buddha-land, retrieve the scriptures, and return home (the *Ci'en Zhuan* differs slightly from this).

A sūtra possesses five aspects: first, the explanation of its name; second, the discernment of its essence (*tattva*); third, the clarification of its thesis (*siddhānta*); fourth, the discussion of its function;

and fifth, the classification of its doctrinal characteristics (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*). Now, phenomena possess names, and names necessarily express an essence. The essence is revealed by means of the thesis, and once the thesis is established, it possesses a function.

By classifying them according to their doctrinal characteristics, they are distinguished and differentiated. In this case, the title uses a metaphor as its name, "True Reality" (*bhūtatathatā*) as its essence, and "Contemplative Insight" (*vipaśyanā*)...

Taking [the realization of] the ultimate truth as its thesis (*siddhānta*), the transcendence of suffering as its function (*prayojana*), and the Mahāyāna as its doctrinal characteristic (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*):

these five are the essential purports within the sutra. The *Prajñāpāramitā* is the Dharma; the word "mind" (*citta*) is the metaphor. This sutra is the sublime, comprehensive meaning of the *Prajñā*.
The metaphor of the human heart-organ (*hrdaya*) represents the primary essence and the fundamental basis of unification. The "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*).
"Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) refers to the mark of emptiness. "Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) means to perceive that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty.
"Crossing over suffering" means to deliver oneself from all suffering and calamity. "Mahāyāna" refers to the profound *prajñā* practiced by Bodhisattvas.
The titles of all sutras do not exceed three categories: person, metaphor, and dharma. A single person refers to works such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha).

A single dharma refers to works such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. A single metaphor refers to works such as the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. Those that combine both person and dharma...
Thus, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others combine both Dharma and metaphor; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others combine persons and metaphor;
and the *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and others combine the three—persons, Dharma, and metaphor.
These include such works as the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* (as seen in the *Yìjùquán*).
The *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the ultimate destination of all practices and the authentic seal of all Buddhas;

therefore, it is taken as the essence (*tattva*). The empty nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is precisely the true mark. To illuminate the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*).

Without illumination, the true mark would not be manifest; therefore, it is taken as the school (*mūla*). Contemplative observation is the cause, and the crossing over from suffering is the fruit. Crossing over from suffering is *prajñā*.
Therefore, it is taken as the functional application.

Regarding the four teachings—the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Complete—this sutra sets aside the Tripitaka and fully possesses the three teachings of Shared, Distinct, and Complete; yet its textual intent lies in the Complete.

It does not preclude the manifestation of the subtle through the inclusion of the coarse; thus, it points out that the aggregates, elements, bases, and entrances are all identical to the true reality (dharmatā). This is explained [in the following].

The "Teaching" (Dharma) refers to the doctrine itself. The term "Mahāyāna" seems to be spoken in reference to the person; for this Dharma is that which is practiced by Bodhisattvas and upon which the Buddhas of the three periods rely. Therefore, it is called Mahāyāna.

The "Contemplation of the Dharma" refers to internal illumination; "mastery" (*vaśitā*) refers to liberation without obstruction. This contemplation is the cause that is cultivated, while mastery is the fruit that is attained.
The "Bodhisattva" is the stage that is realized. (The first phrase serves as the general introduction for the entire passage. "Deep practice" explains what has been attained.

The cause of internal contemplation is "clearly seeing" (insight); the result of the mastery thereby attained is "crossing over suffering" (liberation). This indicates the stage of Bodhisattva attained [thereby].
(These three phrases constitute the general outline of the entire text.)

The Venerable Master Xianshou said: From the beginning, the essential framework is briefly indicated; from the passage "form is not different from emptiness" onwards, the actual meaning is extensively expounded.

Within this, there are five sections: first, dispelling external doubts; second, revealing the essence of the Dharma; third, clarifying that which is to be abandoned; fourth, distinguishing that which is attained;
and fifth, concluding with praise for its superior efficacy.
The Sūtras speak of the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*). First, there is the act of clearly perceiving; there is the practice of profound *prajñā*; and there is Avalokiteśvara.
At this point, one must truly achieve realization. For "Buddha" means awakening; originally, the Buddha did not establish his teachings on the basis of emptiness alone.
If one merely takes the word "emptiness" as a handle, the fault is no small matter. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Emptiness arises within Great Awakening."

It is like a single bubble arising from the ocean. Zibo said that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is merely a medicine prescribed for a specific ailment; once the ailment is gone, the medicine has no further application.
That later generations have labeled the followers of Śākya as the "Gate of Emptiness" is not the true heart-mind of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. This statement is one that must be understood.

The Sūtra takes the simultaneous forgetting of both [subject and object] through wisdom as its ultimate goal; this is the principle of the perfection of empty awakening and the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).

Among the twenty-five perfect penetrations (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) in the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, it uniquely extols Avalokiteśvara’s entry into *samādhi* via hearing, reflection, and cultivation as the standard for practitioners.
This is the very proof of this Sūtra. If students only recognize this mind themselves, then...
All the vehicles of the teachings are for my possession; otherwise, one will be led astray by mere words and will ultimately find no point of entry.

(The commentary on the Sūtra states: "Mind" refers to the originally enlightened true nature, the eternally abiding true mind. All internal mental activity that clings to objects, involving deluded thoughts and discrimination, establishing cognition and views, is the consciousness of the arising and ceasing of the mind;

it is no longer the originally enlightened mind. That which is vividly clear and numinous—the collection of shadows of the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses within—is called the "inner mind. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, which arise in dependence upon external sensory objects and manifest outwardly, is called the "outer mind. Neither of these is the wondrous mind of original enlightenment. Wondrous enlightenment is the...)

It is the mind. This fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind is not within, not without, and not in between. Without true awakening, one cannot realize it; thus, in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the mind was sought in seven locations, yet none were found to exist.

The six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are the root of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The six sense objects combined with the six sense organs constitute the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), which are the locations of the five aggregates.
The six consciousnesses together with the preceding twelve bases constitute the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), which are the constituent divisions of the five aggregates.
Although they are variously distinguished and given different names, they do not, in total, transcend the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). (Eye, ear, nose, tongue...)

The body, form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch constitute the dharma of form (*rūpa-dharma*). The mind constitutes the dharma of mind (*citta-dharma*). As for dharmas, they consist of half-mind and half-form; this is because the "intention" within the mind discriminates the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) to give rise to the characteristics of dharmas.

From "emptiness is devoid of form" up to "neither wisdom nor attainment," it clarifies that from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) through the Great Vehicle, one must in all cases realize that these aggregates are empty of dharmas in order to return to the true essence.

This discourse concerns the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*). "Truth" (*satya*) means reality. It refers to the fact that within the three realms there is actual suffering, and beyond the three realms there is actual bliss;

that there is an actual cessation (*nirodha*) to be realized, and an actual path (*mārga*) to be cultivated. Because one has not yet awakened to the principle of the Mahāyāna illusion-like samādhi, they are called the Four Truths.
Xunzhu said: Someone asked, "If the attainment of wisdom (*jñāna-prāpti*) is precisely the realization of reality, why do you say it does not exist?

He replied, "When one correctly illuminates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there is no emptiness outside of what is illuminated, and no illumination outside of emptiness. It is like space merging with space, or like water being poured into water.

If there were an attainment of wisdom, an obstacle would immediately arise. Therefore, Prajñā takes non-attainment as its core principle. Wisdom is not something that possesses names or characteristics; to cling to the mark of a single wisdom is [an error]."

That which belongs to delusory appearances is false appearance; that which maintains a single view of wisdom is false view. This sutra was originally taught for those of superior faculties who cultivate the Supreme Vehicle. For a practitioner at the initial stage, it is precisely necessary to rely upon this to generate the bodhicitta, seeking wisdom and attaining its realization.
One must not dismiss this as mere deluded thought and empty it of meaning.
The Sūtra speaks of eliminating suffering and extends to it the truth that is real and not false.

It is because all worldly beings gather and burn within the fire-house of saṃsāra, undergoing suffering through endless cycles with no time of escape, that the Buddha, dwelling in awakening, feels a most poignant and earnest compassion, hoping—

People awaken to the Way through words, thereby escaping the realms of suffering. Furthermore, fearing that although the teachings are being practiced, those who do not believe remain numerous, he again exhorts them with earnest urgency, demonstrating to them what is true and not false.

People are addicted to the illusory phenomena before them and create all manner of karma; those places where they create pleasure are precisely the places where they create suffering, for they are deluded regarding the truth.

The root of loss lies in this; for ten thousand kalpas one may follow downward through the threshold between humanity and the animal realm, struggling with all one’s might over nothing more than these few matters.

This is why the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma by first expounding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). If a person can recognize suffering, fear it, and refrain from planting the causes of suffering, they will not undergo the fruits of suffering.
General Principles:
This scripture is divided into seven sections, following the ancient editions (Xianshou also divided it in this manner).

Each section is headed with a four-character title to reveal its essential meaning, with the commentary provided above for the reader’s ease of reference. [This follows the thirty-two... of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The same applies to this category.
Although there are many commentaries on this sutra, only a few are worthy of being followed as authoritative. There is a brief sub-commentary by the Tang National Preceptor Xianshou;
an annotated commentary by the monk Zongle (whose name was also Ruqi) of Mingtian Temple; and a prose work by Song Lian of Jinhua.

There is a commentary by the Elder Zibai (named Zhenko, style name Daguan). Ma Sizhen carved a *Lüeshu Xiaochaō* (A Brief Commentary and Small Excerpts), which was compiled by someone from the late Ming period;

it gathers the various schools to serve as a sub-commentary to Xianshou’s *Lüeshu*. While its glosses and explanations are extremely thorough, it still lacks significant elucidation regarding the subtle essence of principle and phenomena (*lishi*).
There is also the *Yiju Quan* (Exegesis of Meaning and Phrases) by the Layman Dayuan Zhang Youyu, which compiles various expositions and is the most detailed and complete.

This work provides a thorough elucidation of the essential principles and profound subtleties regarding phenomena and reality. Recently, the monk Wenrui of Longxing Temple has produced a "Correct Interpretation" (Zhengjie);
as for other views, they are not worthy of circulation and thus their titles are not listed here.

The various commentaries on these sutras are sometimes detailed and sometimes concise, yet none transcend the conventional style of philological glossing; those that elucidate the profound essence of the principles are rarely seen.

Only the *Yijü Quanchuchūzhūběn* (The Meaningful Phrases Transcending All Versions) excels; this compilation gathers the refined words from each volume, making the revelation of the profound essence of the principles its primary aim.
By providing a structural outline and revealing the core tenets, it offers a detailed exposition for each section, thereby enabling the reader to...
It is easy to gain mastery [of the text].
In this compilation, each individual commentary is headed by the title of the work and the name of its author.

As for the general commentary at the beginning of each section, the reason the author's name is not listed is that it was compiled from the *Yìjùquán* (Exegesis of Meaningful Phrases), which is scattered throughout various expositions.
From within these, I have selected several lines or several phrases, interweaving and rearranging them according to my own humble views to form a coherent whole.

The explanations are not uniform, and the writings are not from a single source; therefore, it is difficult to attribute this to a specific title or author. This is not an attempt to appropriate the merit of others.
What has been explained above serves as a thematic outline for each section, analyzing the subtle and piercing through the profound;
therein lies the essential meaning, supplemented by what was not fully reached in the commentaries.
Regarding the various explanations compiled in these notes, all discourses that were excessively lengthy have been abridged.
May readers kindly refrain from taking offense at this truncation.

The general purport of this entire scripture is that which was spoken by the World-Honored One; it is the essential core of the extensive *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras. Therefore, it is titled with the word "Mind.

It sweeps away all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and speaks solely of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It does not concern itself with branches and leaves, but uniquely highlights the root. This is the gateway to Mañjuśrī’s wisdom.
Why is Avalokiteśvara mentioned first? It is precisely because the Buddhas preach the Dharma solely for the purpose of delivering sentient beings from suffering.

Since Avalokiteśvara is a Great Bodhisattva who specializes in delivering others from suffering and calamity, he is specifically mentioned at the outset as a model for the wondrous wisdom of true emptiness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the delivery from suffering and calamity, it does not refer merely to his fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) or thirty-two manifestations (*upāya-kauśalya*).

Regarding the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is sufficient to say the single phrase: "perceiving that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty. One can see from this that suffering and calamity are immeasurable and boundless;
yet, when one investigates their root, it is simply because one does not perceive the emptiness of the aggregates. Therefore, the profound *prajñā* contemplates only true emptiness.
Furthermore, it does not contemplate within one's own mind, but rather instructs Śāriputra to begin contemplation from form (*rūpa*). This is solely because...
The contemplative gates of those of the Two Vehicles and of bodhisattvas at the initial stage of mind mostly fall on the side of nihilistic emptiness.

Some contemplate emptiness by detaching from form; others designate the cessation of form as emptiness. In general, these are called "nihilistic emptiness. This emptiness is a void, a state of total annihilation, devoid of cognition and utility.
It cannot manifest the myriad dharmas; how, then, could it deliver sentient beings from their suffering and distress? Therefore, the teaching instructs people...

Investigate and penetrate from the perspective of form: the Bodhisattva contemplates that form is not substantial form, but is a phantom manifestation according to conditions, no different from true emptiness.
He contemplates that emptiness is not a void of annihilation, but pervades all forms, no different from illusory form.
Since their essence is mutually inseparable, their function is likewise mutually unimpeded. Therefore it is said:
They are not different; yet they still appear as two things. What is not understood is that form takes emptiness as its essence, and emptiness takes form as its function.
They are not two things fused together, nor are they one thing that can be analyzed apart.
It is like a mirror manifesting reflections—the reflection is the mirror itself; it is like waves in water—the water is the waves themselves. This is the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.

When one’s insight reaches this point, one attains mastery and contemplates that no further aggregates remain. Why, then, does he again speak of the four lines concerning the empty nature of all phenomena?
It is because [the realization] is not yet distinct from them; the object of illumination still persists, and there is a fear that people might mistake this for the true mark of emptiness.

This is manifested through the power of illumination and accomplished by human effort. Therefore, it is said that this characteristic of emptiness is precisely the *tathatā* (suchness) self-nature possessed fully by every person.
"Neither arising nor ceasing" refers to the meaning of the eternal and unchanging nature within *tathatā*.
"Neither defiled nor pure; neither increasing nor decreasing" refers to the fulfillment of pure dharmas within *tathatā*, which is ultimately level and impartial.
This is the meaning of "equality. Among all phenomena, it manifests the characteristic of emptiness, enabling people to recognize the Prajñā of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

Since true emptiness is the very nature of True Suchness (*tathatā-svabhāva*), everything is thereby transcended. The subsequent text immediately follows with, "Therefore, within emptiness there is no form," which directly transcends the limits of the phenomenal realm (*dharmadhātu-pramāṇa*).
Beginning from the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it proceeds directly to the statement that there is no wisdom (*jñāna*).
The field where there is neither attainment nor non-attainment—these three characters, "non-attainment," are the very marrow of profound *prajñā*.
The *dharmatā* (real mark) does not reach this point; it is not a *dharmatā* that is merely the absence of marks. Contemplative observation does not reach this point either.

This is not a mere cessation of illumination, but the true illumination. Therefore, this single phrase is specifically set forth to serve as the point of convergence for the "true emptiness" mentioned above, and the root of the "realization of the fruit" mentioned below.
"The mind has no hindrance" comes from the root of having nothing to be attained; "there is no fear or delusion" comes from the root of having no hindrances.
That there are no hindrances is precisely the perfection of practice; therefore, it is repeated once more.
Because there is not a single word of obstruction, one attains ultimate *nirvāṇa* directly.
That Bodhisattvas and Buddhas realize *nirvāṇa* and attain *bodhi* are both based on this non-apprehending *prajñāpāramitā* as their cause.
Is it not fitting, therefore, to call it the Great Divinity, the Great Illumination, the Unsurpassed, and the Peerless? It is inconceivable; it is only the mantra.
This is indeed so. Is not Prajñāpāramitā itself a mantra? It can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.
This correctly expresses that the efficacy of Prajñā is vast and great. However, this has only spoken of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and has not yet spoken of the *Prajñāpāramitā Mantra*.
Without [the mantra], one cannot manifest the subtlety of Prajñā, which transcends words and is free from marks. Therefore, the mantra is spoken.
This is to demonstrate their cultivation. Furthermore, it is necessary to recite mantras to manifest their wondrousness. Can the four words of "gate gate" be explained through written characters?
Can they be conceived or deliberated upon by the mind? If they could be explained or deliberated upon, they could not be called mantras.

This cannot yet be called Prajñā. Only when the paths of thought and reason are cut off and the nature of words is transcended does one correspond with this state where there is neither wisdom nor attainment, the mark of the emptiness of all dharmas. This is the general outline of the entire sutra.
Those who seek liberation should examine it closely.

In the Sanskrit term *prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, *prajñā* corresponds to "wisdom" (*huìzhì*) in the Chinese language; it is the fundamental mind of human beings. It is a designation for that which transcends emotion and leaves behind views—a state of profound stillness and perfect luminosity.
As stated in the *Xunzhu*: "The reason 'wisdom' is not translated [phonetically] is because it is the most honored among the five reasons for not translating."
It is not translated due to its gravity. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Prajñā is ineffable; it is profoundly deep and extremely weighty.
Wisdom (*hui*) is light and superficial, and thus insufficient to correspond to it. *Hui* is one of the five objects of specific mental states (*biéjìng*).

*Prajñā*, however, is without duality or division, without distinction or interruption. Its essence and function are pure; it is suchness (*tathatā*), perfect, of a single flavor, and eternally true. Therefore—
It is called the "First Pāramitā. If one were to reverse this [to refer to] wisdom (*prajñā*), it would be defiled rather than pure;
it would be dualistic rather than suchness (*tathatā*); it would be divisible rather than perfect; it would be distinct rather than truly one;
and it would be subject to cessation rather than truly eternal. Therefore, by retaining the term *prajñā*, its meaning as peerless, matchless, uniquely honored, and uniquely noble finally emerges.
It is complete. When subdivided, there are three types. First is *prajñāpāramitā* as the true nature (*dharmatā*).

It is produced from subtle, refined perceptions that give rise to inversion. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the eleven types of form-dharmas, which do not exceed the two categories of retribution:
the environment and the body. The first consists of the five sense organs and the four great elements; having a shape that can be seen, it is termed the "root-body world."

It is also called the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), which constitutes the primary retribution (*vipāka*). Within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it serves as the direct objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
First, regarding external objects: anything within the ten realms that possesses form and is visible, or possesses characteristics and is nameable, [is included].

This is called the "receptacle world" (*bhājanaloka*), which is the *pariniṣpanna* (dependent) retribution. Within the *ālayavijñāna*, it constitutes the remote objective aspect (*viprakṛṣṭa-viṣaya-bhāga*).

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are shrouded by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); they grasp at form as being true form, clinging to the view of permanence and becoming deluded regarding emptiness. Thus, they perceive form and emptiness as distinct.

The followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) distance themselves from the five aggregates to contemplate emptiness; they cling to the view of annihilation and extinguish form. Thus, they perceive emptiness and...
Form is distinct. The Bodhisattva discards the ordinary person’s mark of self (*ātman*) and eliminates the partial emptiness of the Two Vehicles.

Knowing that illusory form is not [substantial] form and that true emptiness is not [absolute] emptiness, they clarify that they are not different. There is no form apart from emptiness, yet form is itself emptiness;
there is no emptiness apart from form, yet emptiness is itself form. Thus, they clarify that they are identical.
△ Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva perceived that the five aggregates are all empty.
This is not a case where the aggregates are one thing and emptiness another, as if these two were distinct entities; rather, they are of one essence and identical.
Since form (*rūpa*) is the foremost of dharmic characteristics and the first of the five aggregates, in order to explain emptiness, one first takes up form. First, by means of form...
This is formed by the solidification of firm delusive conceptualization; it is the point where sentient beings most easily become attached.
Furthermore, it stands in diametric opposition to the essence of emptiness; it is the most difficult point to reconcile. If one can penetrate this through investigation, [one will realize the truth].

Then the remaining four aggregates will disintegrate like crumbling walls and melt away like ice; this is what is meant by "once one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.
Ordinary people and those of the two vehicles view form and emptiness as two distinct things: they regard form as arising and emptiness as ceasing;
form as defilement and emptiness as purity; form as increase and emptiness as decrease. Thus, conflicting views arise in competition.

From this arises the distinction between turning toward or away from, and the selection or rejection [of phenomena], thereby differentiating the ordinary from the sage and delusion from enlightenment.

Thus, it is said that they are "not different" in order to shatter the dualistic view of form and emptiness as being distinct. Although provisional and shallow bodhisattvas already know that form and emptiness are not different, [this teaching is still necessary].
It is as if one has still not yet ceased viewing form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as two separate things: form is the phenomenon (*dharma*), while emptiness is the principle (*li*);
form is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while emptiness is the nature (*svabhāva*); form is the function (*yòng*), while emptiness is the essence (*tǐ*).

As these two views persist, one expends great effort in harmonizing and integrating them, and exerts much energy in reconciling and dissolving them. Yet the principle and the essence remain ununified, and illumination and function fail to coincide.
It is utterly extinguished; therefore, it is said that "this is precisely it," in order to shatter the dualistic views of form and emptiness.

Ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) recognize form as truly existent, distinct from the void nothingness of emptiness; they thus perceive form as being able to obstruct emptiness, and emptiness as being hindered by form.
Bodhisattvas, however, see all forms as illusory forms, all of which lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This absence of intrinsic nature—

The nature of form (*rūpa*) is precisely the principle of non-self and emptiness (*śūnyatā*). From the very beginning, one does not perceive even a hair’s breadth that can stain or defile emptiness, nor does one perceive even a hair’s breadth that can intermingle with emptiness.
The characteristic of form and the characteristic of emptiness are from the outset without distinction; this is the non-differentiation from emptiness.
This phrase is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) that clarifies the ultimate (*paramārtha*) within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). It reveals...
This is the True Meaning. Those of the Two Vehicles and bodhisattvas at the initial stage perceive emptiness as annihilation, distinct from the defilement of form;
consequently, they seek to extinguish form and return to emptiness, regarding form as an obstacle to emptiness.

Bodhisattvas, however, perceive the emptiness of self-nature as true emptiness, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm. This principle of the emptiness of non-self is omnipresent within all forms. It does not...
One perceives that outside of emptiness there is a defiled form, yet one does not perceive within emptiness a form that can be severed or extinguished.
The essence of emptiness and the essence of form are entirely without change; they are not different from form.

This phrase is a provisional contemplation arising from essence to function, which reveals the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Once one realizes that form and emptiness are not different, then...
One receives a single dharma and does not abandon a single dharma, thereby avoiding falling into the realms of ordinary beings or the Lesser Vehicle.
Thus, one clarifies the ultimate within the conventional and gives rise to function from the essence. Yet, provisional and shallow bodhisattvas cannot avoid treating these as two separate entities;

whether they attempt to synthesize or differentiate, to illuminate or negate, they ultimately cannot reach the stage of universal integration where all is equal, characterized by a single mark and a single flavor. Therefore, once again—
By means of the non-duality of the single essence that is free from dependence, one immediately enters the Middle Way. It is not that form is different from emptiness;
it is not a matter of depending on their union to cause form to return to emptiness. Form is entirely emptiness—what is called "the total identity of phenomena with principle" (shili).
There is not the slightest bit of rationality that does not reside within these phenomena. Emptiness is not different from form; it is not a matter of depending on emptiness to manifest form.

Thus, the entirety of emptiness is form; what is called "the entirety of principle is phenomena" means that there is not the slightest phenomenal characteristic that does not reside within this principle.
Since one has realized that form is emptiness, when one is correctly illuminating [form], it does not preclude negation.
Since one has realized that emptiness is form, when one is correctly negating [form], it does not preclude illumination. This non-duality of negation and illumination is called the Middle Way.
Dhyāna is the foremost sublime contemplation; it reveals the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), also known as the middle truth.
Once the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is dismantled, the remaining four aggregates are likewise not different from this, and likewise are just this.
What is called "the emptiness of the five aggregates" is thus: emptiness is not separate from the five aggregates, nor does one reach this by practicing profound prajñā.
"Can the Great Bodhisattvas of the Other Shore do such a thing?

Śāriputra, the empty characteristic of all dharmas is precisely the self-characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The Commentary states: "Because the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are not singular, they are called 'all dharmas'."
This reveals this emptiness and stillness; therefore, it is called the "mark of emptiness. Zongle stated: "The mark of emptiness refers to the true mark of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
The Bodhisattva further addressed Śāriputra, saying: "Once one has understood all phenomena, their very substance is precisely the true mark of ultimate reality.
The substance of the true mark is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Since there is no arising or ceasing, how could there be defilement or purity? Since...
In stainless purity, how could there be increase or decrease? The *Huìyào* states: "The characteristic of true emptiness is precisely characterized by non-arising and non-ceasing, and so forth.
Zībó says: "This characteristic of emptiness is the clear perception of the emptiness of the five aggregates."
Guangcheng said: "These dharmas" refers, in brief, to the aforementioned five aggregates (*skandha*), and, in detail, to the dharmas of the ten realms.
"The mark of emptiness" is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As the Sūtra says: "The absence of marks and the non-existence of marks is called the true mark.
It also says: "Contemplate all dharmas as empty, which is their true mark. This is precisely that meaning.
"Neither arising nor ceasing; neither defiled nor pure; neither increasing nor decreasing. The commentary states:
The preceding passage explained that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are themselves emptiness. In reality, it is not only the five aggregates;

all phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise empty. While the phenomenal characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are known by everyone, their characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) can [only be realized through...]
Do you understand yet? From the perspective of the dharmas of ordinary beings, it appears that things arise when conditions converge and perish when conditions disperse.
However, this refers to the phenomenal characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas; it is not so regarding the empty characteristic (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.
All phenomena arise from conditions; that which arises from conditions has no intrinsic nature. In reality, all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.

When the conditions for phenomena depart, they cease; their cessation is merely the cessation of conditions. In reality, all phenomena are fundamentally unceasing. Thus, they are neither born nor extinguished.
From the perspective of the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it appears as though there are defilements to be removed and purity to be cultivated;
yet they do not realize that these are spoken of in terms of the provisional characteristics of all phenomena.

If one considers the empty nature of all phenomena, then even while within tainted form, the essence of emptiness remains unstained; and even while within untainted form, the essence of emptiness remains as it was.

This is neither defiled nor pure. From the perspective of the Bodhisattva-dharma, the perfection of all virtues appears as increase, and the exhaustion of all afflictive obstructions appears as decrease;
yet one does not realize that these are spoken of in terms of the conditioned characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) cultivated through dharmas.

If it were the empty characteristic (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas, from the beginning they have never been reached through cultivation or realization; thus, though virtue is full, there is no increase, and since it is fundamentally unchanging and indestructible, there is no decrease.
The exhaustion of hindrances is not a diminution; it is neither increasing nor decreasing. Thus, the mark of emptiness of all phenomena is precisely the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of Prajñā.
It is what is called the eternally abiding and immovable True Suchness Mind (*tathatā-citta*), which is subject to no change or decay.
It is what is called the fundamentally pure and inherently luminous Tathāgatagarbha that pervades the entire Dharma-realm. It is what is called this...
The Dharma is equal; it is the Perfectly Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) in which there is no high or low. Seeking the Pearl, it says:
"If one explains this by directly clarifying the essence of emptiness, the ten realms and the five aggregates are collectively termed 'all dharmas' (dharmas).

From the very beginning, they have been eternally quiescent and extinguished; they are forcibly named 'true reality' (bhūta-lakṣaṇa). True reality is without characteristics, and is therefore called the characteristic of emptiness. Because of birth, extinction, and defilement..."
One seeks them through the increase or decrease of purity, yet they are entirely unobtainable. Because they do not arise, there is no mark of birth-and-death;
because they do not cease, there is no mark of nirvana. Because they are not defiled, there is no mark of affliction; because they are not pure, there is no mark of bodhi.
Because they do not increase, there is no mark of fetters and karma; because they do not decrease, there is no mark of liberation.
△ Master Yixuan says: The preceding passage has already explained that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby implicitly revealing the characteristics of true emptiness.

Fearing that people might fail to grasp this and mistake it for a mere matter of meditative observation, or lack faith in the fact that the true mark (dharmatā) is inherently so, he therefore points out the characteristic of emptiness within all phenomena to ensure they understand.
The original true reality has always been thus. If this aspect of emptiness cannot manifest before one at all times, then when it is perceived, it arises;
when the perception passes, it ceases; when there is illumination, it is pure; when the illumination vanishes, it is defiled; and when the illumination manifests, it increases.
When illumination is severed, it diminishes. To simply say "form is identical to emptiness" is entirely a matter of shadows and reflections;
it cannot be reckoned as the illumination of true wisdom. Therefore, this is specifically clarified. Regarding the search for the pearl, it is said: "This explains the essence by way of emptiness.

It extensively clarifies that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty, and that emptiness is the true mark (*dharmatā*). By means of the six 'nots,' the essence is explained through this fundamental emptiness."

"Regarding its essence": these are words that point directly [to the truth]. "All phenomena" (*dharmas*) encompasses what follows: the bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), the truths (*satya*), conditions (*pratyaya*), and the perfections (*pāramitā*).

The "characteristic of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) is the wondrous characteristic of true emptiness; it is the numinous clarity beyond all dependence, the true emptiness in which there has been no thing from the very beginning.
This is precisely the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena. [Appendix: Correct Explanation] Because all phenomena accord with the mind, they appear to arise.

There is cessation. Ordinary people perceive that their physical bodies undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death; that the realms of the sensory world undergo formation, subsistence, decay, and emptiness;
and that the conscious mind undergoes arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. Only this essence of true emptiness is fundamentally quiescent and ultimately firm;

therefore, it is said to be neither born nor extinguished. This demonstrates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Because they become attached to emptiness and weary of existence, [the teaching] is divided.

Regarding defilement and purity: the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive that the gate of transmigration within the triple world, as well as the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), are the aspects of defilement;
whereas the gate of cessation and return beyond the triple world, as well as the two truths of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), are the aspects of purity.

Consequently, they avoid the turbid and evil environments of the five corruptions and pursue the biased emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Yet, within this wondrous existence of true emptiness, the ten realms are level.

...and so forth. Therefore, it is said to be "neither defiled nor pure. This demonstrates the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Because the two extremes are in mutual opposition, there is increase and decrease.
The Bodhisattva practices severance—namely, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) to overcome stinginess and greed, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) to overcome ignorance, and so on.

Through this, as one perceives and attains the True Principle, it gradually becomes perfected; the delusions and obstructions gradually vanish. Only this essence of wondrous existence within true emptiness [remains]. For all...

The Sage is perfectly integrated; both the real and the false are extinguished. Hence it is said that there is neither increase nor decrease. This demonstrates the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*), yet to categorize it as the "contemplative object" (*guan-jing*) is not in accord with the principle.

Let this remain for consideration. The correct interpretation states: The three contemplations (*san-guan*) in the preceding section demonstrate the true vision (*zhen-jian*) that shatters the false vision (*wang-jian*).
The three truths (*san-di*) in this section demonstrate the true aspect (*zhen-xiang*) that shatters the false aspect (*wang-xiang*).
"Therefore, in emptiness.
Regarding this, "therefore" refers back to the preceding context. "In emptiness" means within that aforementioned emptiness which is neither-arising-nor-ceasing and so forth.
Within that true emptiness, there are no dharmas such as the five aggregates and so on; this clarifies true emptiness.

This is the departure from marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Searching for the pearl, it says: "This [passage] begins above and extends below, extensively clarifying that the true emptiness of *prajñā* contains neither worldly nor world-transcending phenomena.
Regarding "beginning above," this refers to the character "no" (*wu*) here, which follows from the six instances of "not" (*bu*) above.

Regarding "extending below," this refers to the four characters "therefore, in emptiness" (*shìgù kōngzhōng*), which flow in a single breath all the way down to "no wisdom and no attainment" (*wúzhì wúdé*).
This sentence is a discourse on the true emptiness of non-arising and non-ceasing within the primary root. Therefore, the characters "is" (shi) and "therefore" (gu) are attached.
The *Jijie* states: "Emptiness (kong) is the Ultimateless (wuji). Within emptiness lies the Ultimateless, which is the Great Ultimate (taiji)."
There is no form; there is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

This is the emptiness of the five aggregates. Zongle says: Within this true reality of ultimate emptiness, one cannot seek it through arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase or decrease; therefore, he concludes by saying: "No form; no feeling, perception, mental formations..."
Regarding "consciousness and so forth," the *Jíjiě* (Compendium of Explanations) states: "Emptiness is the true essence that is neither born nor extinguished.

Within this true essence, how could there arise the names and characteristics of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? Regarding the search for the pearl, it says: "The previous [verse] illuminated the emptiness of the five aggregates.
From the perspective of the person, this speaks of being empty of the five aggregates; from the perspective of their nature, [it refers to the nature of] Xianxiu."
It says: "The absence of form and so forth, and the absence of letters, are spoken of as being contrary to the meaning of emptiness.

In reality, however, none of these destroy form and so forth, because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*) and thus do not depend on destruction. The following passages should be understood accordingly.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental object.
Since the five aggregates do not exist, neither do the six sense organs nor the six sense objects. This is the emptiness of the twelve bases (*āyatana*). The text states:
"Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are called the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*); they are like the roots possessed by grasses and trees. [The eye...]
Seeing is the dust-object of form; hearing by the ear is the dust-object of sound; smelling by the nose is the dust-object of fragrance; tasting by the tongue is the dust-object of flavor;
touching by the body is the dust-object of tangibility; and mental attachment is the dust-object of phenomena. These are the six dust-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).

They are like the obscuration of fine dust and sand, for they defile the pure mind of man; therefore, they are called "dust. When these dust-objects and the sense-faculties combine, they constitute the twelve [bases].
*Āyatana*. *Āyatana* means "place" (*so*). It signifies that each has its own location. Buddhayaśas says:

The old translation was "twelve entrances" (*dvādaśāyatana*), meaning the six sense organs and six sense objects mutually enter into one another. The new translation is "twelve bases" (*dvādaśāyatana*), meaning that the internal organs and external objects each have their own specific locations.
When a practitioner uses them daily, they should illuminate these organs and objects; their essence is precisely *prajñā*, which is suddenly empty.
Because it is Perfect Enlightenment, it is said to be non-existent.
There is no realm of the eye, and so on, up to no realm of mental consciousness.
Since the twelve bases do not exist, neither do the eighteen realms. As for the eighteen realms, they consist of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six...

This refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). By citing the first and last realms, the sixteen intermediate ones are omitted; thus, the terms "from... up to" (*yāvat*) are used merely to abbreviate the text.
The *Wenju* states: "From seeing arises eye-consciousness; from hearing arises ear-consciousness; from smelling arises nose-consciousness;
from tasting arises tongue-consciousness; from contact with objects arises body-consciousness; and from discrimination arises mind-consciousness."

These are called the six consciousnesses. "Consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the deluded arising of discrimination that obscures true wisdom. "Sphere" (dhātu) refers to a delimited domain. As the *Xunzhu* says:
"The six consciousnesses discriminate the six sense objects; by clinging to the deluded, differences are formed, each having its own boundary."

These are called the eighteen *dhātus*. Although both the three [groups] and the six [groups] are mentioned together, the emphasis lies on the six consciousnesses. The six consciousnesses are fundamentally but a single consciousness;

however, they are designated as six based on the different functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. It is like a monkey that must respond at six windows; thus, they are named the six consciousness-elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*).
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that a person has eight consciousnesses: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and...
The first five consciousnesses correspond to the sensation (*vedanā*) aggregate among the five aggregates; this is the function of these five consciousnesses.

The sixth consciousness is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which corresponds to the perception (*saṃjñā*) aggregate among the five aggregates; this is the function of this mental consciousness.

The seventh and eighth consciousnesses have names but no substantial form; they are lodged within the six [consciousnesses]. Specifically, the seventh is the transmitting consciousness, which is the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*). This is...
That which moves the mind and flows on without ceasing is the function of *saṃskāra* among the five aggregates.

That which contains and stores is the *ālayavijñāna*, which corresponds to the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) within the five aggregates and the term "consciousness" within the twelve links of dependent origination discussed below; both belong to this consciousness.
It is the root of the six kinds of consciousness, as it is said: "The single essence of brilliance divides and becomes [the six]."
Sixth, the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*). ○ Zongle said: "The three categories mentioned above do not transcend the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

For those whose delusion regarding the mind is predominant, they are taught as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); for those whose delusion regarding form is predominant, they are taught as the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*);

and for those deluded regarding both mind and form, they are taught as the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). Those who practice and study should, according to their respective faculties and capacities, simply..."

Cultivating this single section, one immediately attains awakening and entry. The correct interpretation states: The above three sections clarify that there are no dharmas of the aggregates, sense bases, or elements;
this is the severing of ordinary delusions.
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; likewise, there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.
This is the emptiness of the twelve links of dependent origination. Ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions...

There is. Conditioned by existence (*bhava*), there is birth (*jāti*). Conditioned by birth, there are old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair; these are also called the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*).

Their mutual dependence is termed "condition" (*pratyaya*); their distinct branching is termed "links" (*aṅga*). Furthermore, by mentioning the beginning and the end while omitting the middle, it is said "up to and including.
Beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*) and ending with old age and death, this is the arising through causes and conditions. They arise in successive order. That is to say:
"Thus arises this entire mass of suffering. This is what the Buddhist scriptures call the "sequential contemplation of the process of arising" (*anuloma-pravṛtti-dvāra*).

From the exhaustion of ignorance to the exhaustion of old age and death, there is the cessation of causes and conditions. Their cessation in successive order is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
This is what the Buddhist scriptures call the "sequential contemplation of the process of cessation" (*pratiloma-nivṛtti-dvāra*). Cessation is synonymous with exhaustion. Zongle said: "This..."
The twelve links of dependent origination encompass the causes and effects of the three periods of time.

Through their successive mutual dependence, the single thought-moment of ignorance stirs the ocean of *tathatā*, causing the whirlpool of birth and death to revolve like a wheel. All sentient beings are deluded and do not realize this;
it is the objective realm contemplated by those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle. In the Mahayana Prajñāpāramitā, one penetrates through to the ultimate emptiness. Pure...
Within this single great treasury of radiant light, how could there be so-called transmigration and cessation, or various distinctions and sequences?
Therefore it is said: "Non-existent. It is said: "Exhausted. According to the explanations in the *Yan yi quan* and the *Xun zhu*, the fundamental nature of wisdom is inherently luminous.
The wondrous, profound, and luminously pure [mind] suddenly becomes obscured and dark due to the fleeting arising of deluded thoughts;

therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). From this point on, it flows and wanders without ceasing. As seen in its activities, it creates various kinds of karma. Thus, regarding "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise":
because of ignorance, the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) arises, which discriminates objects and serves as the seed for future births. By means of these three links, they constitute the root.
Fundamentally, these [factors] give rise to the subsequent nine links to constitute the conditions of the three periods of time.

The two links of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) serve as the causes of the past, while consciousness (*vijñāna*) marks the initial point of reliance for the effects of the present. As the illusory form begins to fade away, the spiritual consciousness immediately hastens forth;
it enters and takes refuge in the mother’s womb, receiving the designations of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the matter of physical form. Therefore...

It is said that consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Once name-and-form exists, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are consequently complete within the womb, possessing the function of entering into contact with objects;
therefore, it is said that name-and-form conditions the six sense bases. Once the six sense bases exist, upon emerging from the womb, they immediately encounter the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*);
therefore, they condition contact (*sparśa*). Once there is the sensation of contact, there is the experience of suffering and pleasure within the mind; therefore...
Conditioned by feeling (*vedanā*). These five factors above are the fruits experienced in the present.
Once the mind has experienced them, it craves various excellent requisites and sensual pleasures; therefore, it is conditioned by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Since there is craving, one pursues objects without ceasing, giving rise to a mind of grasping toward those objects; therefore, it is conditioned by grasping (*upādāna*). Through craving, one grasps, and the mind becomes attached.
One rushes about in pursuit, thereby creating various karmas of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*). Therefore, it is said that "clinging conditions becoming" (*upādāna-pratyaya-bhava*).
These three links constitute the causes produced in the present life. Through these fetters of existence, one becomes the cause for birth within the three realms;
in a future life, one again undergoes birth among the four modes of birth and the six destinies. Once there is birth, there must necessarily be aging and death. From this...
Samsara has no end. These two branches are the fruits to be experienced in future lives.

The preceding passage on the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) was explained horizontally, as being fully present at one time; this explains the essence of the twelve links of dependent origination.
This current explanation of the twelve links vertically describes them as causes and effects across the three periods of time; it explains the aggregates, elements, and so forth.

Cause and effect is called the gate of transmigration (*pravṛtti-mukha*). To know that transmigration arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) and that it should cease starting from the cessation of ignorance, continuing until old age and death—where all causes and conditions are extinguished together—is called the gate of cessation (*nivṛtti-mukha*).

This gate of transmigration is the cause for the realization of emptiness by the *pratyekabuddha* through contemplation; this gate of cessation is the cause for the cultivation of the realization of emptiness by the *pratyekabuddha*. This...
This is also the method for entering cultivation through awakening; within emptiness, however, there is no such dharma.
As for the Pratyekabuddhayāna, one attains the Way from this and transcends the triple world.
There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path;
this is the contemplation of the purity of the Four Noble Truths. Seeking the pearl, [one finds that] suffering has oppression as its characteristic.

this exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Second is the sensation of pleasure (*sukhā-vedanā*), which gives rise to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); this extends through both the desire and form realms (*rūpadhātu*). Third is the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

It can give rise to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), which extends throughout the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). As for the eight sufferings: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of aging; third, the suffering of illness;
fourth, the suffering of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from the beloved; sixth, the suffering of encountering the hated;

seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks—these seven are enumerated collectively to constitute the eighth, the suffering of the intense proliferation of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha-saṃskāra-duḥkha*), also known as the suffering of the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha-duḥkha*).

If categorized according to the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*), the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) comprises five of the eight sufferings: namely, birth, death, old age, sickness, and association with the unpleasant, as well as those phenomena conducive to painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanīya-dharma*).

The suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) comprises two of the eight sufferings: namely, the unattainability of what is sought and separation from the beloved, as well as those phenomena conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanīya-dharma*).

The suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) comprises one: namely, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha-duḥkha*), as well as those phenomena conducive to neutral feeling (*upekṣāvedanīya-dharma*). (From the *Shuchao*).
It is said: A Great Sūtra states that suffering has immeasurable characteristics, which are not known by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

This is because, although the followers of the two vehicles know the characteristics of suffering, they do not know its immeasurable characteristics; thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of one hundred and twenty [characteristics] of suffering.
This is clarified by increasing the number to forty-four in the *Catuścatvāriṃśat-sāhasrikā-śāstra*. Xianshou said:
"Because it excludes the certainty of suffering, it is called 'true and not false. Yiquan said:
"All methods for eliminating suffering through worldly cultivation, practice, and merit are merely provisional skillful means; they are not the true, ultimate Dharma-gate. Only this [Dharma-gate]..."
If its power and function can indeed bring about ultimate liberation from suffering, it is truly not false.
Those who wish to deliver themselves from all suffering and calamity—could they possibly fail to enter through this Dharma-gate?

Regarding the traditional interpretation of "Great Deity" and "Great Brilliance," one should incorporate into the discourse such phrases as "sweeping away the lairs of afflictions," "subduing the demonic armies of birth and death," and "transforming the ordinary into the sagely."
It seems as though the intention is to invade and transcend suffering and distress; yet, upon reaching the phrase "transcending suffering," it appears redundant and flavorless.
The Great Power and Great Wisdom merely illuminate that which precedes the attainment of non-intelligence.

While discussing principles in an abstract manner, it is more clearly defined and truly not hollow to include both *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi* within the section on transcending suffering, following immediately after the discourse on transcending suffering.
The *Jíjiě* (Compendium of Explanations) says: This sutra ultimately returns to the removal of all suffering; it is true and not false.
It simply does not fall into the realm of arising and ceasing, but rather attains a genuine, practical realization. Yìquān (Yìxuān) says:
These four lines of the Great Divine Mantra—from "Form is not different from emptiness" to "no wisdom, no attainment"—are spoken from the perspective of their profound and vast meaning.

The two lines, "Exhorting others to practice can eliminate all suffering," speak of the most immediate points for applying effort within the two stages of the root [of cyclic existence] and nirvāṇa-bodhi, in order to exhort others to accept them with faith. The *Wenju* states:
"This section praises the excellence of the empty truth of prajñā; it consists of urgent words of exhortation."
△ Continuing from the preceding text: All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have realized the ultimate fruit by relying upon this *prajñā*.
Therefore, one should know that this *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be sought through language or written characters, nor can it be reached through conceptualization or discrimination.
Relying solely on the words of the sutra is insufficient to manifest its subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence. It is not...

It is sufficient to manifest its supreme excellence and universal pervasiveness. Within the Buddha-dharma, there is nothing more secret in its functional application, nor more efficacious in its spiritual response, than mantra.
The Prajñāpāramitā is itself nothing other than mantra. Mantra is the esoteric speech spoken by the Buddha;
it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It possesses the power of inconceivable transformation, such that no one knows its full extent.
"Opportunity" (*ji*): No sentient being knows its cause. Therefore, it is used to praise *prajñā*. From "True and not false" onwards, the preceding text praises *prajñā* through explicit exposition;
the concluding praise is treated as implicit. From the recitation of the mantra (*dhāraṇī*) onwards, the main text contains both the explicit and the implicit;
the explicit exposition of the secret mantra serves as the general conclusion. The four lines beginning with "Great Deity" (*mahādeva*) refer to the essence (*tattva*).
Praising the Secret [Mantra]. The two phrases "able to eliminate" refer to praising the secret according to its function;
therefore, he speaks the *prajñāpāramitā* mantra. He then spoke the mantra, saying:
*gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
△ Continuing from the preceding text: Since Prajñā possesses such efficacy, Prajñā is itself a mantra (*dhāraṇī*).
However, were it not for the recitation of the mantra, one could not manifest the subtlety of Prajñā—its transcendence of words and its severance from marks.

Therefore, having already expounded the Sūtra to demonstrate its practice, the mantra is further expounded to reveal its subtlety. In other scriptures, the Sūtra is the Sūtra and the mantra is the mantra; [here, they are unified].
The sūtras reveal the exoteric and the esoteric; thus, the sūtras have the name "sūtra," and the mantras have the name "mantra.

Now, however, Prajñāpāramitā is itself the mantra—exoteric is itself esoteric—and the mantra is itself Prajñāpāramitā—esoteric is itself exoteric. The name of the sūtra is itself the name of the mantra; the two meanings of exoteric and esoteric are not divided.
The mantra is the secret speech of all Buddhas, not to be understood by those at the stage of a cause (bodhisattvas); one should simply...

Recite and uphold [this mantra]. It removes obstacles and increases merit; it cannot be explained by force. Should one wish to explain it by force, I shall briefly interpret it according to the traditional meaning:
*gate* means "to go" or "to transcend"; *pāragate* means "truly and not falsely," which refers to the function of profound wisdom.
That is to say, it is the removal of all karmic obstacles, the transcending of all suffering and distress, and the returning to reality. Thus, the term *gate* is repeated.
"Self-deliverance and deliverance of others. *Pāramitā*: "Pāra" is translated here as "the other shore," which refers to the place reached by crossing over.
*Pārasaṃmitā*: "Saṃ" means "totality," "multitude," or "universality"; it refers to reaching the other shore collectively, both for oneself and for others.
As for the term "bodhi," to what kind of other shore does one arrive? It refers to...
It is the locus of Great Bodhi. As for the term *svāhā*, this is translated as "swiftly.
By means of this *prajñā*, one attains bodhi; it is thus rapid and free from obstruction. ○ Xunzhu says: The *Fahua shu* states:
Regarding the meaning of mantras: some masters say they are the names of the kings of spirits;

by invoking the name of such a king, his clan honors him as their lord, and thus one is able to subdue all malevolent spirits—this is the *sarvamaṇḍala* of the world of spirits. Others say that a mantra is like a secret signal within an army;
when the signal is called out and corresponds [to the recipient], there is no need for questioning or interrogation—this is the *sarvamaṇḍala* of humans. Or it is said:

"Mantra" (dhāraṇī) refers to the secret, silent subduing of evil; thus, evil naturally ceases. Others do not understand this. This is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the definitive doctrine of antidotes).
Alternatively, it is said that a mantra is like a secret command within an army, known only by the commanding general while all others remain unable to fathom it.

By analogy, a mantra is known only by the Buddha, while those of other ranks cannot comprehend it; this is the primary *siddhānta*. Furthermore, "mantra" means "aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*). It is like the [parasitic] *gongming* wasp...

The cicada prays to the larvae of the *mingling* moth, wishing that they become like itself. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas pray that all sentient beings may all attain perfect enlightenment just as they have.孤山 (Gushan) says:
"If one seeks deeply the underlying principle, it is merely a subtle expression of this Prajñā mind of non-attainment.
It corresponds with the empty nature of all phenomena, being without wisdom and without attainment."
A person should maintain this with the mind alone; do not rely on the mouth. Maintain it with single-minded focus, without distraction. Do not forget it, nor force it.

Continue until you reach the stage where there is nothing to be attained. Then, through silent resonance, realize this *prajñā* of the emptiness of the aggregates—the mind that has nothing to be attained.
This causes people to give rise to great wisdom. There is nothing that surpasses this secret path, wherein there is nothing to be attained yet all is attained.
One who upholds the mantra should act in this way; likewise, one who practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā is also thus.
